report.source_text: On examination in the neurosurgical clinic, the patient had hyperaesthesia from the neck down, most prominent in the hands and groins. The patient had reduced grip strength of 3/5, finger extension and abduction of 3/5, wrist flexion and extension of 3/5, elbow flexion of 4+/5, elbow extension of 4/5 and shoulder abduction of 4+/5 on the Medical Research Council power scale. Hip flexion was 3/5, with all other muscle groups in the lower limb at 4+/5. The patient had very brisk reflexes with pathological spreading in the upper and lower limbs. There was self-limiting clonus in the ankle bilaterally. Hoffmann’s and Babinski reflexes were positive bilaterally. There was a severe loss of coordination and balance. Gait was impaired; the patient required a frame to mobilise.

report.source_text: The patient underwent MRI imaging and was found to have multilevel degenerative changes of the cervical spine. At C3/4 there was a broad-based disc osteophyte protrusion causing compression of the spinal cord with T2 hyperintense signal changes within the cord. At C5/6, there was a broad-based disc osteophyte protrusion with mild narrowing of the C6 neural foramina (figure 1).

report.source_text: The patient was recovering well on review 3 months post-surgery. Cervical spine radiographs demonstrated appropriate position of her spinal implants. Her wound had healed well. She reported reduced sensory problems and reduced paraesthesia in her fingers. On examination, compared with pre-surgery power, grip strength had improved to 4+/5, wrist flexion and extension had improved to 4/5 and elbow flexion, extension and shoulder abduction had improved to 5/5. Finger extension and abduction remained 3/5. Power had improved to 5/5 in all muscle groups in the patient’s lower limbs. The remainder of the examination was unchanged.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 62-year-old woman presented with a 3-year history of progressive dysaesthetic sensory symptoms (feelings of water retention, gel infiltration, hair stuck down) and motor decline, including multiple falls, right leg giving way, gait disturbance, stiff legs, urinary and faecal incontinence, reduced manual dexterity, and numbness/tingling in upper limbs. She had presented to the ED on 11 occasions over 3 years. On neurosurgical examination, she demonstrated hyperaesthesia from neck down (most prominent in hands and groins), significant upper limb weakness (grip 3/5, finger extension 3/5, wrist flexion/extension 3/5), lower limb weakness (hip flexion 3/5), very brisk reflexes with pathological spreading, bilateral ankle clonus, positive Hoffmann's and Babinski reflexes bilaterally, severe ataxia, and impaired gait requiring a frame. MRI cervical spine revealed multilevel degenerative changes with a broad-based disc osteophyte protrusion at C3/4 causing spinal cord compression with T2 hyperintense signal changes (indicating myelopathic cord changes), and additional protrusion at C5/6 with mild C6 neural foraminal narrowing. She underwent anterior cervical discectomy at C3/4 for surgical decompression. At 3 months post-surgery, she demonstrated significant neurological recovery with improved grip strength (4+/5), wrist flexion/extension (4/5), elbow and shoulder strength (5/5), full recovery of lower limb strength (5/5 in all muscle groups), reduced sensory symptoms and paraesthesia, and well-healed surgical wound with appropriate spinal implant positioning.

Surgical decompression performed via anterior cervical discectomy at C3/4
